subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Resolve x³/((x − a)(x − b)(x − c)) into partial fractions.

mark_split.label: Divide, then set up the form

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.68 — SAQ chapter 11 Partial Fractions, answer 104. Printed appearances: TS 16, 19; AP 16. ⚠ THE 1+1+1+1 SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — this chapter prints no [N Marks] tags against any answer, only tick boxes. The split is the four moves of the method (set up the form · clear the denominators · find the constants · write the result), one mark each, and the SAME split and the SAME step ids (s1_form, s2_identity, s3_constants, s4_result) are used on all fifteen cards of this unit, deliberately: they are one method over different fractions. For the improper fractions the division lives inside s1_form, and for the (x − 3)³ question the substitution x − 3 = y takes the place of the form. The book's SAQ chapter header carries ★★★ and reads '4 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-2A Section B runs Q11–Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q15 is the Partial Fractions slot (the chapter has no Section A or Section C slot). Model Paper 5 (book p.119) asks exactly this question at Q15. No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper — recorded, not hidden. The book's final line prints the third constant with a lowercase c, 'c(x − a)(x − b)', in its identity; it is the constant C, and the card writes C. The book states A and then writes 'similarly' for B and C; the card writes all three so the pattern (each letter's cube over the differences from the other two) is visible. Truth check: with a = 1, b = 2, c = 3 the constants are A = 1/2, B = −8, C = 27/2, and putting x = 0 in the identity gives 0 = (−1)(−2)(−3) + (1/2)(−2)(−3) + (−8)(−1)(−3) + (27/2)(−1)(−2) = −6 + 3 − 24 + 27 = 0.

recall_prompt: Say how you would resolve x³/((x − a)(x − b)(x − c)) into partial fractions — name each move in order, starting with what must be done before the form is written.
insider_note: Equal degrees give the constant quotient 1 — no long division needed — and each constant follows one pattern: the letter cubed over its differences from the other two, so B's denominator is (b − a)(b − c), never a copy of A's.

steps.label: Divide, then set up the form
steps.margin_note: First mark. Degree 3 over degree 3: improper. Both leading coefficients are 1, so the quotient is the constant 1. Then one constant over each of the three different linear factors.

recall.must_convey: That equal degrees make the quotient the constant 1, and the form is 1 + A/(x − a) + B/(x − b) + C/(x − c).
accept: the degrees are equal so the quotient is one, then write one plus A over x minus a plus B over x minus b plus C over x minus c
improper with equal degrees so a constant one comes first and then one constant over each factor
one plus A by x minus a plus B by x minus b plus C by x minus c
degrees same kabatti quotient one, tarvata A by x minus a plus B by x minus b plus C by x minus c rasali
write the constant one and then three fractions for the three linear factors

steps.why: The denominator expands to x³ + …, so x³ over it is 1 plus a proper fraction. The 1 must be written into the form; the letters a, b, c change nothing about the method.
common_mistakes: Writing A/(x − a) + B/(x − b) + C/(x − c) with no 1 in front.
Trying to expand (x − a)(x − b)(x − c) fully and do a long division; with equal degrees the quotient is read off the leading coefficients.
Using a, b, c as if they were numbers to be found; they are given constants.

steps.label: Clear the denominators
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Multiply by (x − a)(x − b)(x − c). The 1 keeps the whole denominator; A keeps (x − b)(x − c), B keeps (x − a)(x − c), C keeps (x − a)(x − b).
lines: + A(x − b)(x − c) + B(x − a)(x − c)

recall.must_convey: That multiplying through gives x³ = (x − a)(x − b)(x − c) + A(x − b)(x − c) + B(x − a)(x − c) + C(x − a)(x − b).
accept: multiply both sides by all three factors to get x cubed equals the whole denominator plus A into x minus b into x minus c plus B into x minus a into x minus c plus C into x minus a into x minus b
clear the denominators and the one keeps the whole denominator while each constant keeps the other two factors
x cubed equals the product plus A B C times the other two factors each
moodu factors tho multiply cheste x cube equals whole denominator plus A B C into migatha rendu factors
remove the fractions and keep the one term as the full product

steps.why: The quotient 1 is a term of the equation and is multiplied by the denominator like the fractions. Each constant is left with the two factors it does not sit over, ready to be isolated.
common_mistakes: Dropping the (x − a)(x − b)(x − c) term that comes from the 1.
Giving A the factor (x − a) that it sits over.
Writing lowercase c for the constant C, which the book does in its own final line.

steps.label: Find the constants
steps.margin_note: Third mark. x = a makes the product and the B and C terms zero: a³ = A(a − b)(a − c). The same pattern with x = b and x = c. Each constant is that letter cubed over its differences from the other two letters.
lines: Put x = a: a³ = A(a − b)(a − c)
Put x = b: B = b³/((b − a)(b − c))
Put x = c: C = c³/((c − a)(c − b))

recall.must_convey: That x = a gives A = a³/((a − b)(a − c)), and likewise B = b³/((b − a)(b − c)) and C = c³/((c − a)(c − b)).
accept: put x equals a to get A equals a cubed over a minus b into a minus c, and the same way B equals b cubed over b minus a into b minus c and C equals c cubed over c minus a into c minus b
each constant is that letter cubed divided by its differences from the other two letters
A is a cube by a minus b a minus c, B is b cube by b minus a b minus c, C is c cube by c minus a c minus b
x equals a pedithe A equals a cube by a minus b into a minus c, alage B and C
substitute the three roots a b and c to get the three constants

steps.why: The roots are a, b and c themselves. Substituting x = a makes every term with (x − a) vanish, which is the product and the B and C terms, leaving a³ = A(a − b)(a − c). B and C follow by the same one-line move.
common_mistakes: Writing A = a³/((a − b)(a − c)) and then B with the same denominator instead of (b − a)(b − c).
Forgetting that at x = a the product (x − a)(x − b)(x − c) is zero and keeping it on the right.
Writing a² instead of a³ in the numerator; the left side is x³ at x = a.

steps.label: Write the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The 1 comes first, then each constant over its own factor. The result is four terms and too long for one box, so the constants are boxed under it.

lines.text: ∴ A = a³/((a − b)(a − c)); B, C likewise

recall.must_convey: That the fraction equals 1 + a³/((a − b)(a − c)(x − a)) + b³/((b − a)(b − c)(x − b)) + c³/((c − a)(c − b)(x − c)).
accept: the answer is one plus a cubed over a minus b a minus c x minus a plus b cubed over b minus a b minus c x minus b plus c cubed over c minus a c minus b x minus c
one first then each constant over its own factor x minus a x minus b x minus c
write one plus the three fractions with a cube b cube and c cube on top
final answer one plus a cube by a minus b a minus c x minus a plus b cube by b minus a b minus c x minus b plus c cube by c minus a c minus b x minus c ani rasali
put A B C back into the form with the one in front

steps.why: The constant quotient 1 and the three fractions together are the resolution. Each fraction has its constant written out in a, b, c over its own factor; that is what the examiner marks.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the 1 in the final line.
Writing A/(x − a) without replacing A by a³/((a − b)(a − c)).
Not checking: take a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, so A = 1/2, B = −8, C = 27/2; put x = 0 in the identity, 0 = −6 + 3 − 24 + 27. If the two sides differ, a constant is wrong.
